stem:
In the diagram, lines $p$ and $q$ are parallel and transversal $t$ crosses them. Angle $a$ measures $65^\circ$. Angle $b$ is alternate to angle $a$.

Which claim about angle $b$ is correct?

options.text: Angle $b$ equals $65^\circ$ only when $t$ is perpendicular to $p$ and $q$.
Equal alternate angles $a$ and $b$ are what create the parallel marks on $p$ and $q$.
Angle $b$ equals $65^\circ$ because alternate angles formed by a transversal of parallel lines are equal.

teacher.key_rationale: With p ∥ q cut by transversal t, alternate angles are equal, so b = a = 65°. Requiring a right-angle transversal, reversing angles as creators of parallelism, or taking the supplement (co-interior) all miss the alternate-angle hinge.
teacher.figure_note: Rewrote source triangle figure as parallel lines p,q with matching arrows, transversal t, and alternate angles a and b.
